# Code review iteration

Reviewed tact-app/web at commit `b641bdc 2023-08-22`: full read of manifests (package.json, tsconfig.json, next.config.js, .babelrc, Dockerfile, .npmrc), CI workflows, the API/IndexedDB data layer (`services/`), the MobX store layer (`stores/`, per-component `store.ts` files), helpers, and representative pages/components — 356 TS/TSX files total. Review angle: real defects first, then idiomaticity against the current (2026) TypeScript 5.x / React 18–19 / Next.js ecosystem, then toolchain currency. No previous review files existed in `.github/reviews/`; all findings below are new.

Severity: **Crit** / **High** / **Med** / **Low** / **Nit**.
Class: `correctness` · `security` · `concurrency` · `perf` · `api` · `idiom` · `modern` · `test` · `build` · `docs`.

## 1. Root store is recreated on every provider render

`stores/RootStore/index.tsx:120-137`

```tsx
export function RootStoreProvider({ children, router }) {
  const store = new RootStore();      // line 127: new store every render

  if (isClient) {
    store.init();                     // line 130: async side effect during render
  }
  ...
  store.setRouter(router);
```

`RootStoreProvider` constructs a fresh `RootStore` in the component body with no `useState`/`useRef` memoization. The provider re-renders at minimum once per page load (it consumes `useUser()`, which flips when the Auth0 profile resolves) and again on every route change (it is rendered directly by `App` in `pages/_app.tsx`). Each re-render therefore: (a) throws away the entire store tree — `SpacesStore`, `TagsStore`, `GoalsStore`, `MenuStore`, modal controller state; (b) re-runs `init()`, which re-reads all spaces/tags/goals from IndexedDB and flips `isLoading` back to `true`; (c) performs async side effects during the render phase, which is illegal under React 18 concurrent rendering and StrictMode. Any state that lives only in memory (open modals, menu state) is silently lost on navigation. The `getProvider` helper (`helpers/StoreProvider.tsx:52-63`) has a milder variant of the same disease: it constructs stores and calls `update()` inside `useMemo`, which React explicitly does not guarantee to cache.

**Fix.** `const [store] = useState(() => new RootStore());` (or `useRef`), move `store.init()` into `useEffect(() => { store.init(); }, [store])`, and move `store.setRouter(router)` into an effect as well. In `getProvider`, construct the store with `useState(() => ...)` and keep `update()` in the existing effect only.

## 2. POST requests are sent with the GET method

`services/api/ApiService.ts:26-37`

```ts
post = <R>(url: string, params?: Record<string, any>, options: RequestInit = {}) => {
  return fetch(resolveUrl(url), {
    ...options,
    body: JSON.stringify(params),
    method: 'GET',                    // line 34: copy-paste from get()
  }).then((response) => wrapResponse<R>(response));
};
```

A GET request with a body makes `fetch` throw `TypeError: Request with GET/HEAD method cannot have body` in browsers, so every `post` call — task creation, bulk creation, task map lookup — would fail unconditionally. The bug is latent today only because `RootStore` wires up `IDBService` (which overrides all four verbs) instead of `ApiService` (`stores/RootStore/index.tsx:78`), meaning the entire fetch-based class is currently dead code with a broken method waiting for the day a real backend is connected. Note also that no request sets `Content-Type: application/json` and `wrapResponse` discards the response body on errors, keeping only `statusText`.

**Fix.** Change to `method: 'POST'`, add a JSON `Content-Type` header in one place, and include the response body (or at least status code) in thrown errors. Add a smoke test so a dead-code path like this cannot silently rot.

## 3. Toolchain and dependencies are frozen in mid-2023

`package.json:60` (`"next": "^13.4.19"`), `tsconfig.json:3-13`, `.babelrc:1-7`, `.github/workflows/ci.yml:46-59`

The stack is consistently two-plus years out of date, and several items are past end-of-life or formally deprecated:

- **Next.js 13 (pages router)** — EOL; multiple security fixes have landed only in 14/15 (including the middleware authorization-bypass class of issues patched in later lines). React 18.2 predates React 19.
- **Node 18** (engines, Dockerfile `node:18-alpine`, CI `node-version: 18`) — EOL since April 2025.
- **`tsconfig.json`: `strict: false`, `target: es5`** — the codebase visibly pays for this: implicit-`any` parameters throughout (`middleware.ts`, hotkey handlers), unchecked nulls. TS 5.x-era code is strict by default; `es5` as a target is obsolete for an app that only runs in evergreen browsers.
- **`.babelrc` with `@babel/plugin-proposal-class-properties`** — a deprecated proposal plugin for a feature that has been standard since ES2022; the custom Babel config also opts the whole build out of Next's SWC fast path.
- **`react-beautiful-dnd`** — deprecated and archived by Atlassian; it does not support React 18 StrictMode and will not support React 19.
- **`moment`** — in maintenance mode; used here for a single `format()` call (`helpers/DateHelper.ts`) plus goal date math.
- **`@tanstack/react-virtual` pinned at `3.0.0-beta.54`** — a beta of a library that has long since shipped stable 3.x.
- **`pre-commit` npm package** (last published ~2016) is the only enforcement of lint/type-check.
- **CI actions `actions/checkout@v3`, `actions/setup-node@v3`** — superseded by v4/v5 (v3 runs on a deprecated runner runtime).
- **`uuid` v9** — `crypto.randomUUID()` is built into all supported runtimes now.

**Fix.** Migration outline, in dependency order: (1) Node 20/22 + actions v4/v5 in CI and Dockerfile; (2) TypeScript strict mode on (start with `strict: true` + targeted `// @ts-expect-error`, or ratchet per-flag), `target: es2022`, drop `.babelrc` in favor of SWC (MobX class fields work with `useDefineForClassFields` and mobx's documented config); (3) Next 14 → 15 on the pages router (mechanical), React 18.3 → 19; (4) replace `react-beautiful-dnd` with `@dnd-kit` or `pragmatic-drag-and-drop`, `moment` with `date-fns`/`dayjs`/Temporal, stable `@tanstack/react-virtual`, drop `uuid` for `crypto.randomUUID()`; (5) replace the `pre-commit` package with lefthook/husky and add npm auditing (dependabot already covers npm — good) plus `npm audit`/osv-scanner in CI.

## 4. CI never runs lint or type-check and there are zero tests

`.github/workflows/ci.yml:63`, `package.json:13-20`

The only quality gate in CI is `npm run build` plus a depcheck run. `npm run lint` and `npm run type-check` exist as scripts but are wired solely to the abandoned `pre-commit` npm package, i.e. they run only on the machines of contributors who happen to have the git hook installed — trivially bypassed with `--no-verify` and never enforced for PRs. There is not a single test file in 356 TS/TSX sources: no unit tests for the non-trivial store logic (focus/keyboard state machines in `TodayStore`, list bookkeeping in `TasksListStore`), no component tests, no e2e. Bugs like [[#2. POST requests are sent with the GET method]] and [[#8. Wont-do reason is persisted only for the first selected task]] are exactly the kind that a thin test layer catches at commit time.

**Fix.** Add `lint` and `type-check` steps to `ci.yml` (they are cheap and already scripted). Introduce Vitest + React Testing Library; start with the pure store layer (`TasksListStore`, `ListNavigation`, `Validator`) where tests need no DOM, then add one Playwright smoke flow (create task → complete task) to guard the IndexedDB data layer.

## 5. IndexedDB data is not scoped to the authenticated user

`services/api/Database/index.ts:64` (`openDB<MyDB>('tact-db', 5, ...)`), `pages/today/index.tsx:16` (`withPageAuthRequired`)

Pages are gated behind Auth0, which signals an expectation of per-user data privacy — but every user's tasks, goals, and descriptions are written to a single browser-wide IndexedDB database named `tact-db`. On a shared machine, user B who logs in after user A sees all of user A's tasks; logging out clears the Auth0 session but leaves the whole task database readable on disk and via the app itself. Authentication is effectively decorative with respect to the data it appears to protect.

**Fix.** Key the database (or a top-level object-store namespace) by the Auth0 `user.sub` — e.g. `tact-db/${sub}` — and delete or detach local data on logout (`onRedirecting`/logout callback). If the local-first single-user model is intentional for now, document it prominently and drop the misleading auth wall, or gate it behind an explicit "this device stores data locally" consent.

## 6. Emoji data is fetched from a third-party CDN at runtime

`stores/EmojiStore/index.tsx:24-33`

```ts
const response = await fetch(
  'https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/@emoji-mart/data'
);
this.emojiData = await response.json();
```

A production app makes a runtime request to jsDelivr for executable-adjacent content that is not pinned to any version or integrity hash. This is a supply-chain and availability liability (CDN outage or a compromised package release breaks or poisons the picker), leaks user IPs to a third party, and the code never checks `response.ok` — a 404/500 flows into `response.json()` and surfaces as an unrelated parse error caught by the blanket `catch`. The store also never resets `isLoading` on failure, so a transient error permanently wedges the picker for the session.

**Fix.** Add `@emoji-mart/data` to `dependencies` and import it statically (or via `import()` for code splitting) so it ships versioned inside the bundle. If a remote fetch must stay, pin the exact version in the URL, check `response.ok`, and reset `isLoading` in a `finally`.

## 7. Font Awesome token is baked into the build-stage environment

`Dockerfile:5-6`

```dockerfile
ARG token
ENV FONTAWESOME_TOKEN=${token}
```

The private registry token is passed as a build `ARG` and then promoted to `ENV`, which persists it in the build-stage image config and layer history (`docker history`, cache exports, any registry that receives the intermediate stage). The final `prod` stage does not inherit it, but shared build caches and `--target build` images leak it. The file already opts into BuildKit via `# syntax=docker/dockerfile:latest`, so the proper mechanism is available.

**Fix.** Use a BuildKit secret: `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=fontawesome FONTAWESOME_TOKEN=$(cat /run/secrets/fontawesome) npm ci ...` and build with `--secret id=fontawesome,env=FONTAWESOME_TOKEN`. Drop the `ARG`/`ENV` pair entirely. (Bonus: `COPY --from=BUILD` relies on case-insensitive stage matching of the `build` stage — spell it identically.)

## 8. Wont-do reason is persisted only for the first selected task

`components/shared/TasksList/store.ts:552-563`

```ts
setTaskWontDoReason = (ids: string[], reason: string) => {
  ids.forEach((id) => {
    this.items[id].wontDoReason = reason;

    if (!this.delayedCreation) {
      this.root.api.tasks.update({
        id: ids[0],                    // line 558: always the first id
        fields: { wontDoReason: reason },
      });
    }
  });
};
```

Inside the per-id loop the API update is issued with `ids[0]` instead of `id`. With a multi-selection, the first task's reason is written N times and every other task's reason exists only in memory — it silently disappears on the next `loadTasks()` or page reload. The in-memory UI shows the reason on all tasks, so the data loss is invisible until later.

**Fix.** Use `id` in the update payload, and hoist the `delayedCreation` check out of the loop. Consider a bulk endpoint (`tasks.update` already accepts `fields`) to avoid N sequential writes.

## 9. Async promise executor swallows every data-layer error

`services/api/Database/IDBService.ts:62-70`

```ts
fakeRequest = <T>(method, url, arg) => {
  return new Promise<T>(async (resolve) => {
    const stub = this.stubs[method][url];
    const db = await this.getDB();
    const result = stub ? stub(db, arg) : null;
    resolve(result);
  });
};
```

An `async` function as a `new Promise` executor is a classic anti-pattern (`no-async-promise-executor` in ESLint): if `getDB()` or a stub throws, the rejection happens inside the executor's async function — the outer promise never settles, callers `await` forever, and the error surfaces only as an unhandled rejection. Since this method fronts literally every read/write in the app, any IndexedDB failure (quota, private-browsing restrictions, upgrade conflict) manifests as an eternal spinner with no Sentry breadcrumb. Note also that `stub(db, arg)` returns a promise which is passed to `resolve()` un-awaited — errors from the stub itself are equally unobserved by this layer. Relatedly, the schema `upgrade` callback in `services/api/Database/index.ts:66-113` wraps every `createObjectStore` in `try {} catch (e) {}`, masking real migration failures instead of switching on `oldVersion`.

**Fix.** `fakeRequest = async (method, url, arg) => { const stub = ...; const db = await this.getDB(); return stub ? stub(db, arg) : null; }` — plain async method, no executor. Let errors propagate and add a single error boundary/Sentry capture at the store layer. Rewrite `upgrade` to check `oldVersion`/`db.objectStoreNames` instead of blanket try/catch.

## 10. Variable-length dependency array and destructive singleton teardown

`helpers/GlobalHooksHelper.ts:66-80`

```ts
useEffect(() => { ... }, [
  isInitialized,
  hooksWithCallbacks,
  params.updateWhenRemoved,
  GlobalHooksStore.isEventListenerCreated,
  GlobalHooksStore.isEventListenerRemoved,
  ...dependencies                       // line 74: spread into deps
]);

useEffect(() => {
  return () => GlobalHooksStore.destroy();   // line 78
}, []);
```

Two Rules-of-Hooks violations in one hook. First, spreading a caller-supplied array into the dependency list means the array length can change between renders, which React treats as undefined behavior (it compares slots positionally and warns/misfires when the size changes). Second, `GlobalHooksStore` is a module-level singleton with a single `globalHooksCallbacks` slot: every mounted component that calls `useGlobalHook` overwrites the previous component's callbacks (last-one-wins), and when any one of them unmounts, its cleanup calls `destroy()`, removing the global `keydown` listener for everyone still mounted. Whether hotkeys work after closing a modal depends on mount order.

**Fix.** Replace the singleton with reference counting (register returns an unregister function; the document listener is added on first registration and removed on last), key registrations by component, and take a fixed-shape dependency (the callbacks object memoized by the caller) instead of a spread array.

## 11. MobX state is mutated outside actions after awaits

`components/shared/TasksList/store.ts:449-452`, `components/pages/Today/store.ts:703-707`, `stores/RootStore/Resources/GoalsStore.ts:198-201`

```ts
await Promise.all([
  Promise.resolve().then(() => this.items[task.id] = task),  // mutation in a microtask
  this.delayedCreation ? null : this.root.api.tasks.update(...),
]);
```

`makeAutoObservable` wraps methods in actions, but an action's transactional scope ends at the first `await`. Patterns used throughout — `this.focusModeConfiguration = await this.root.api...` (`Today/store.ts:704`), `this.map = await this.root.api.goals.list()` (`GoalsStore.ts:199`), and the `Promise.resolve().then(...)` mutation above — all mutate observables in untracked async continuations. Under MobX 6's default `enforceActions: "observed"` this emits dev warnings, defeats transaction batching (observers fire per-assignment mid-flight), and the microtask variant additionally reorders the local write relative to the API call for no benefit. This is the single most repeated MobX idiom violation in the codebase.

**Fix.** Use `runInAction` around post-await assignments (the codebase already does this correctly in `loadTasks`, `store.ts:589-594` — make it the house style), or convert loaders to `flow`/generators which keep action semantics across yields. Delete the `Promise.resolve().then` wrapper and assign directly.

## 12. Deep imports reach into react-hotkeys-hook internals

`helpers/useHotkeysHandler.ts:1-6`, `helpers/ListNavigation.ts:3-5`, `next.config.js:3`

```ts
import { Options, useHotkeys } from 'react-hotkeys-hook/src';
import { HotkeysEvent, OptionsOrDependencyArray } from 'react-hotkeys-hook/src/types';
```

The app imports the library's un-built `src/` directory instead of its public entry point, and `next.config.js` carries `transpilePackages: ['react-hotkeys-hook']` solely to compile those internals. This couples the app to the package's private file layout — any upstream refactor (or a move to `exports` maps, which most libraries have since adopted and which block deep imports outright) breaks the build even on a patch upgrade, and it forfeits the library's published, tested build. All types used here (`HotkeysEvent`, `Options`) are exported from the package root in current 4.x/5.x versions.

**Fix.** Import from `'react-hotkeys-hook'`, drop `transpilePackages`, and upgrade the package (current versions also changed `enableOnFormTags` semantics — retest the hardcoded override in `useHotkeysHandler.ts:118`, which currently force-enables all hotkeys inside inputs and relies on each store's `enabled` flag to compensate).

## 13. useRootStore guard checks undefined but the default is null

`stores/RootStore/index.tsx:111-121`

```ts
export const StoreContext = createContext<RootStore>(null);

export function useRootStore() {
  const context = useContext(StoreContext);
  if (context === undefined) {          // line 116: never true
    throw new Error('useStore must be used within StoreProvider');
  }
```

The context default is `null`, so outside a provider `useContext` returns `null`, the `=== undefined` guard never fires, and the caller gets a `null` store that explodes later with an unrelated `Cannot read properties of null`. The safety net is dead code. The generic `getProvider` variant is worse: it defaults to `{} as StoreType` (`helpers/StoreProvider.tsx:37`), so a missing provider yields an empty object and silent undefined-method behavior instead of any error at all.

**Fix.** `createContext<RootStore | null>(null)` and guard with `if (!context)`. In `getProvider`, default to `null` and throw in `useStore` — with `strict: true` (see [[#3. Toolchain and dependencies are frozen in mid-2023]]) the compiler will enforce the narrowing.

## 14. Middleware runs on every request without a matcher

`middleware.ts:3-9`

```ts
export async function middleware(req, ev) {
  const { pathname } = req.nextUrl;
  if (pathname == '/') {
    return NextResponse.redirect(new URL('/today', req.url));
  }
  return NextResponse.next();
}
```

Without an exported `config.matcher`, this edge function is invoked for every request — all static assets, `_next/*` chunks, images, API routes — just to test for `/`. That is wasted edge invocations (billed on Vercel) and added latency on every asset. The function is also untyped (`req`, `ev` are implicit `any` — `NextRequest` exists for this) and needlessly `async`, and `==` instead of `===` survives only because ESLint's `eqeqeq` is not enabled.

**Fix.** Add `export const config = { matcher: '/' };`, type the signature `(req: NextRequest)`, drop `async` and the unused `ev`. Alternatively delete the middleware entirely and use a `redirects()` entry in `next.config.js`, which is handled at the routing layer for free.

## 15. The j and k navigation keys are inverted

`helpers/ListNavigation.ts:49-54`

```ts
UP: ['up', 'j'],
DOWN: ['down', 'k'],
...
FIRST: ['meta+up', 'meta+j', 'h'],
LAST: ['meta+down', 'meta+k', 'l'],
```

In every established j/k convention — vim, Gmail, GitHub, Linear (the app's evident inspiration) — `j` moves down and `k` moves up. Here they are swapped, so muscle memory from every other tool does the opposite of what the user expects. `h`/`l` as first/last is likewise nonstandard (vim uses them for left/right), which is at least a deliberate choice, but the j/k swap reads as a plain transposition bug.

**Fix.** Swap the bindings: `UP: ['up', 'k']`, `DOWN: ['down', 'j']`, and mirror the change in `FIRST`/`LAST` (`meta+k` / `meta+j`).
